title: Jollof Rice and Chicken
author: Ozoz Adeniyi
desc: The household version — basmati pre-soaked twenty minutes, no parboiling, no foil, 800 ml of liquid to 500 g of rice, and the smoke if it happens is an accident.
longDesc: This is the same author's everyday jollof and it contradicts her party version on almost every structural point. Basmati rather than long grain, pre-soaked at least twenty minutes rather than parboiled, no foil under the lid, and no deliberate burn — she notes that the rice may stick and even burn, that some people in Nigeria consider that the best part, and that it does lend a smoky barbecue flavour, but it is described as something that happens rather than something you do. Six tomatoes and half a chilli, with no sweet pepper at all.
ingredients: 500 g long grain or basmati rice, about 6 teacups, rinsed and drained
6 medium fresh tomatoes, or 400 g tinned tomatoes
1/2 or less fresh chili, to taste
2 tbsp coconut or vegetable oil, or butter
steps: If you are using basmati, pre-soak it at least 20 minutes. Rinse and drain.
Blend the tomatoes, 2 onions and the chili until smooth.
Heat the oil, add the sliced onion and stir-fry 1 to 2 minutes.
Add the blended mixture, the tomato puree, curry powder and thyme, and season with salt. Cook 10 to 12 minutes on medium.
Add the water or stock, stir and season.
Add the rice, stir, cover and bring to the boil.
Add the butter, stir, reduce the heat and steam 15 to 20 minutes until cooked.
If it is too dry, add stock or water and stir gently.
When cooked, remove from the heat and cover the pot opening with a tea cloth before serving.
chefTips: Pre-soak basmati at least twenty minutes. The author's own note is that it does taste quite different from parboiled long grain, and she prefers it.
Eight hundred millilitres to five hundred grams of rice. That is the clearest liquid-to-rice ratio of the three documented jollofs.
Season well up front and give it a good stir at the beginning — her own tip, and it matters because you will barely stir it again.
Cook on low heat, do not over-stir, and do not add too much liquid at a time. That is the whole of her technique advice.
No foil under the lid here, and no parboiling. If you want the party technique, it is NGA109 — and note that recipe rules out the basmati this one prefers.
Six tomatoes to half a chilli and no sweet pepper at all. That makes this a markedly more tomato-led jollof than the party version.
The tea cloth over the pot opening at the end absorbs condensation. Same finish as the party version.
commonMistakes: Adding liquid in large amounts partway through.
Expecting party-jollof smoke from a method that does not produce it deliberately.
sources: Adapted from 'Jollof Rice and Chicken', published on kitchenbutterfly.com. ATTRIBUTION: the byline prints as the site name, not 'Ozoz Sokoh'; the site is credited, with Sokoh noted as proprietor.

Quantities exactly as printed: 2 tablespoons coconut/vegetable oil/butter; 6 medium fresh tomatoes or 400g tinned tomatoes; 3 medium onions (1 sliced, 2 blended); 1/2 or less fresh chili, to taste; 1 tablespoon tomato puree; 2 tablespoons curry powder; 2 teaspoons dried thyme; 1 stock cube; 500g long grain or basmati rice (about 6 teacups, rinsed and drained); 800ml water or stock; 2 tablespoons butter; optional mixed herbs, shrimp, meat chunks. Yield not stated.
HER RICE POSITION, verbatim: she uses basmati rather than traditional parboiled long-grain — 'I pre-soak it for at least 20 minutes before I cook with it. It does taste quite different.'

THE SMOKE IS AN ACCIDENT HERE, verbatim: 'Note that when cooking, the rice may stick to the bottom of the pan…..and even burn. Now, some in Nigeria consider this the best part of the meal…..scooping up every burnt grain onto their plates. I must admit that sometimes, it lends a smoky, bbq-like flavour to the rice.' Contrast the party version, where the burn is a deliberate 3-to-5-minute step (NGA109).
HER TIPS, verbatim: 'Season well up front and give good stir at the beginning. Cook the rice on low heat, dont over stir and don't add too much liquid at a time.'
On stock, as printed: 'Add about 1/2 – 1 litre of boiling water to the mixture, which is left after the chicken is cooked to make the stock. Strain in a sieve…keeping the liquid for the Jollof rice!'

On crayfish in jollof, which is contested, verbatim: 'the answer is yes….sometimes, Jollof rice has crayfish in it, depending on who makes it. I skip it in mine…not liking fishy rice!' Neither of the other two documented jollofs uses it.

THE SAME AUTHOR'S TWO JOLLOFS CONTRADICT EACH OTHER and this is the single clearest example in the collection of one cook publishing two different dishes under one name. Here: basmati preferred, no parboil, no foil, accidental smoke, 6 tomatoes to half a chilli with no sweet pepper. At Food52: long grain explicitly 'not basmati', a 12-to-15-minute parboil, double foil under the lid twice, a deliberate 3-to-5-minute burn, and 6 tomatoes to 6 poblano to 1 scotch bonnet. Not reconciled — the party version is the technique document and this is the household one.
No foil or leaf lid is used here; the lid alone, with a tea cloth at the end.
reheating: Steam, or microwave with a splash of water under a damp cover.
healthBenefits: Tomato-led, so high in lycopene, which becomes more available once cooked.
Basmati has a lower glycaemic index than most parboiled long grain.
Moderate in fat for a jollof.
culturalNote: Household jollof and party jollof are not the same dish and this pair of recipes proves it from inside one kitchen. The everyday version is quicker, more tomato-forward and cooked in a normal pot with a normal lid; the party one is a production with foil, staged stock and a deliberate burn. Both are honestly jollof, and the burnt grains at the bottom are prized either way.
